name: Denningvleis
summary: Sweet-sour Cape Malay lamb stew, slow-cooked with onions, bay, allspice and tamarind until the meat falls from the bone in a dark, glossy gravy.
about: One of the oldest dishes of the Cape Malay kitchen; its name is usually traced to the Malay word dendeng, spiced meat. The sour once came from tamarind, still sold in Cape Town spice shops, with vinegar as the home substitute. It is cooked for special occasions and Sunday tables and served with yellow rice and raisins.
steps: Heat the oil in a large heavy-based pot over medium-high heat and brown the lamb in two or three batches, about 4 minutes a batch, until well coloured on all sides. Lift each batch onto a plate.
Turn the heat to medium, add the onions, bay leaves, allspice and cloves to the same pot and fry, stirring now and then, until the onions are soft and deep golden, 12 to 15 minutes.
Stir in the garlic and chilli and fry for 1 minute, until fragrant.

Return the lamb and its juices to the pot, pour in the boiling water and bring to a simmer. Cover, turn the heat to low and cook gently for 1 hour, stirring every 20 minutes and adding a splash of water if it starts to catch.
Meanwhile soak the tamarind pulp in 4 tbsp hot water for 10 minutes, squeeze it through your fingers, then strain the liquid and throw away the seeds and fibre.
Stir the tamarind liquid, brown sugar, nutmeg, salt and pepper into the stew. Cover and simmer on low for another 45 minutes to 1 hour, until the lamb is tender enough to pull from the bone.

Take the lid off for the last 10 minutes so the gravy reduces and turns thick and glossy. Taste: it should be gently sweet and sour, so add a little more sugar or tamarind to balance. Remove the bay leaves and whole spices and serve hot with yellow rice.
prepNote: Tastes even better the next day; cool, refrigerate for up to 3 days and reheat gently with a splash of water.
